clue.text: Extremely demure and modest, yet showing allure

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremities of the word demure, its first and last letters

parts.note: modest means coy, shy and retiring

explanation.surface: A demure, modest woman who is nonetheless alluring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'demure', giving DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A decoy is a lure or bait, something that entices, which is what an allure is as a noun.

clue.text: Without breaking down, active people succeed remarkably

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so one piece is placed around the other

parts.note: people who are active, who get things done, are doers

indicators.note: breaking signals that the word down is smashed and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who never collapses, among busy people, achieves great things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' scrambles 'down' to WOND; 'Without' is the old sense of outside, not lacking, so the active people go around it.
explanation.definitionFit: To do wonders is an idiom for achieving remarkable results.

clue.text: Piece of writing for a section of society

explanation.surface: A writer's work aimed at one part of society.
explanation.definitionFit: A book is divided into numbered parts of text; a local branch of a club or society is also so named.

clue.text: Swift creation bringing yell of excitement

explanation.surface: An invention by someone quick that makes people whoop.
explanation.walkthrough: Swift is Jonathan Swift, whose Gulliver's Travels features brutish humans of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Swift invented these brutes in Gulliver's Travels, and the word is also a whoop of delight.

clue.text: Confronts state as way to avoid disgrace

parts.note: to confront someone is to face them, so confronts gives faces
to state is to assert or aver

explanation.surface: A politician faces down the government to escape shame.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that saves one's face spares one humiliation, a means of escaping dishonour.

clue.text: Weapon a soldier has to discharge initially

indicators.note: initially says the firing piece comes at the beginning, before the soldier pieces

parts.note: to discharge a gun is to fire it
RM stands for Royal Marine, a soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier must shoot his gun first.
explanation.walkthrough: RM is a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: A firearm is a gun, a weapon that shoots.

clue.text: Possible addition beneath facade, for example

definitions.text: Possible addition beneath facade, for example

parts.words: Possible addition beneath facade, for example
parts.note: the word facade can be spelt with a little hook under its c, an accent mark added beneath a letter

explanation.surface: Something that might be built under the front of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests building works beneath a frontage; the 'addition' is the hook under the c of façade.
explanation.definitionFit: This mark sits beneath a c, as in façade, to show it is pronounced soft.

clue.text: Reluctant to buy, accepts one new line

indicators.note: new signals a fresh arrangement of the letters before it

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A doubtful shopper takes on a new range of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges ACCEPTS plus I and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Being doubtful means not believing a claim, idiomatically not 'buying' it.

clue.text: Fragrant plant from boy accepted by girl

indicators.note: accepted by means taken in by, so the boy's name goes inside the girl's

parts.note: Vera is a girl's name
Ben is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A girl receives a sweet-smelling flower from a boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbena is a garden plant prized for its scented flowers.

clue.text: Dangerous run — I hit ball high in the air

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for run in cricket scores

parts.words: hit ball high in the air
parts.note: in cricket, to sky the ball is to hit it steeply upward

explanation.surface: A batsman admits that his lofted shot was reckless.
explanation.walkthrough: To sky a ball, in cricket and other sports, is to hit it very high.
explanation.definitionFit: Something risky carries the chance of harm.

clue.text: Outside at present, .we had survived

indicators.note: outside means the first piece goes around the others

parts.note: we had contracts to we'd
present means here, in attendance

explanation.surface: We spent time outdoors at the moment and got through it.
explanation.walkthrough: WE'D (we had) goes outside AT plus HERE.
explanation.definitionFit: To have weathered a storm is to have come through it intact.

clue.text: Money in, thus, a Continental way coming over here?

indicators.note: coming over means turning round, so the run of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: thus means so
rue is French for street, a way on the Continent

explanation.surface: Wondering whether European currency will cross the Channel to Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming over' reverses the whole run, giving the letters backwards. The clue dates from 1999, when Britain adopting the single currency was hotly debated.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the currency of most EU countries.

clue.text: Form of gambling I try — one not at all complicated

indicators.note: complicated means mixed up, so the letters of the preceding words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A punter says the game he tries is really easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complicated' rearranges I TRY ONE NOT AT ALL. Britain's National Lottery began in 1994.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's state-run lottery is a game of chance on numbered draws.

clue.text: What could make me a lord?

definitions.text: What could make me a lord?

indicators.note: could make suggests the letters can be rearranged to produce something else

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what would get them ennobled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could make' rearranges ME A LORD; the whole clue also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer's title and rank is what being raised to an earl's estate would give.

clue.text: Dustman rarely led to toil?

explanation.surface: A refuse collector who seldom gets round to working.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Doolittle is the dustman in Shaw's Pygmalion (and My Fair Lady); the second sense is the phrase 'do little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Doolittle is Shaw's dustman; someone seldom drawn to work would do little.

clue.text: Praise current class having objective

parts.note: AC is alternating current
CL is an abbreviation for class
an objective is an aim

explanation.surface: A teacher commends the present class for having a goal.
explanation.definitionFit: Acclaim is enthusiastic public approval.

clue.text: Form of golf that's light entertainment

explanation.surface: A type of golf that is just easy fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf scored by holes won is the first sense; playing with a lit match would be light play.

clue.text: Reported easy game and what supporters do

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the word is said out loud

parts.note: someone who is easy game is a dupe, a sucker

explanation.surface: Fans are said to enjoy an easy game and their support.
explanation.definitionFit: To give help and comfort, as backers do.

clue.text: Brainbox caught associating with non-U element

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: non-U says the letter U is to be left out of the next word

parts.note: uranium is a chemical element

explanation.surface: A clever person is found mixing with a lower-class crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class, which misleads here.
explanation.definitionFit: The skull is the box that holds the brain, a punning sense of 'brainbox'.

clue.text: Cause a car crash, leading to arrest

indicators.note: leading says the arrest piece goes in front of the other

parts.note: to run someone in is slang for arresting them

explanation.surface: A driver causes an accident and is then detained.
explanation.walkthrough: RUN IN, informal for arrest, goes before TO.
explanation.definitionFit: To collide with another vehicle is to drive into it.

clue.text: Try to obtain what's correspondingly allowed by law

parts.note: correspondingly means so, likewise
licit means lawful

explanation.surface: Seeking only what the law equally permits.
explanation.definitionFit: To ask for or seek something, as when requesting business.

clue.text: Dear fruit

explanation.surface: An expensive piece of fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A term of endearment like darling, and a variety of grapefruit hybrid.

clue.text: Advise an amusing character

explanation.surface: Telling an entertaining person what to do.
explanation.definitionFit: To warn someone, and informally a person who is a real card.

clue.text: It's written in full like this

definitions.text: It's written in full like this

parts.words: It's written in full like this
parts.note: in a bar order such as gin and it, the it is short for a drink, here spelt out in full

explanation.surface: A clue that seems to describe the spelling out of a word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as in 'gin and it' is short for this Italian fortified wine.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'gin and it', 'it' abbreviates the sweet red fortified wine from Italy.

clue.text: Writer, having assembled nibs and pen, starts off

indicators.note: starts off means the opening letters of the two words are removed

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An author gathers his writing implements and gets going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts off' removes the first letter of each of 'nibs' and 'pen', leaving IBS and EN to join.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright.

clue.text: Maiden on island welcoming a call from Tom?

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in, so a letter goes inside the island

parts.note: IOW is the Isle of Wight, an island off southern England

explanation.surface: A young woman on an island greets a phone call from a man called Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom is a tomcat, not a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's cry; a tom is a male cat.

clue.text: Source of sin isn't commonly one of these

definitions.text: Source of sin isn't commonly one of these

indicators.note: the source of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: ain't is the colloquial form of isn't

explanation.surface: A holy person, as people say, is no origin of wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: S plus AIN'T; the whole clue describes a holy person.
explanation.definitionFit: A holy person is by definition no origin of wickedness.

clue.text: Name Alan, in the novel, had

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are given a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A character in a book had the name Alan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges ALAN IN THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathaniel is a man's first name.

clue.text: Naval officer who's looked after without regard for others?

definitions.text: who's looked after without regard for others?

explanation.surface: A selfish naval officer who looks after himself.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Royal Navy this is the first lieutenant; 'looking after number one' means putting yourself first.
explanation.definitionFit: Navy slang for a first lieutenant; also oneself, in 'look after number one'.

clue.text: Nervous and verbose

explanation.surface: Someone anxious and long-winded.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for scared, and also meaning long-winded or full of empty talk.
